claim: Greater mouse-eared bats use two foraging strategies with similar average nightly captures of 25 small, aerial insects and 29 large, ground-dwelling insects per bat.
source: We show that these bats use two foraging strategies with similar average nightly captures of 25 small, aerial insects and 29 large, ground-dwelling insects per bat, but with much higher capture success in the air (76%) vs ground (30%).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from biologging tags recording prey captures across 34 bats, as shown in Figure 1D and described in the Results section.

claim: Greater mouse-eared bats have much higher capture success in the air (76%) versus ground (30%).
source: We show that these bats use two foraging strategies with similar average nightly captures of 25 small, aerial insects and 29 large, ground-dwelling insects per bat, but with much higher capture success in the air (76%) vs ground (30%).
evidence: Success ratios were calculated from audible mastication sounds following prey captures, as described in the Methods and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: 85% of the nightly food acquisition comes from ground prey despite the 2.5 times higher failure rates.
source: However, owing to the 3–20 times larger ground prey, 85% of the nightly food acquisition comes from ground prey despite the 2.5 times higher failure rates.
evidence: This is calculated from prey body mass estimates (DNA metabarcoding and mastication analysis) combined with capture success data, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: Ground prey are 3-20 times larger than aerial prey.
source: However, owing to the 3–20 times larger ground prey, 85% of the nightly food acquisition comes from ground prey despite the 2.5 times higher failure rates.
evidence: Prey sizes were estimated from DNA metabarcoding and body length measurements, showing ground prey averaged 20 mm vs 7 mm for aerial prey (Figure 3C).

claim: Most bats use the same foraging strategy on a given night.
source: We find that most bats use the same foraging strategy on a given night suggesting that bats adapt their hunting behavior to weather and ground conditions.
evidence: Statistical analysis (LMM) showed that the night of tagging explained the ratio between ground and aerial captures (Supplementary file 1g, Figure 1D-E).

claim: Bats adapt their hunting behavior to weather and ground conditions.
source: We find that most bats use the same foraging strategy on a given night suggesting that bats adapt their hunting behavior to weather and ground conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that bats tagged on the same night chose similar foraging strategies, suggesting environmental factors influence foraging decisions.

claim: Greater mouse-eared bats use high risk-high gain gleaning of ground prey as a primary foraging tactic.
source: We conclude that these bats use high risk-high gain gleaning of ground prey as a primary foraging tactic, but switch to aerial hunting when environmental changes reduce the profitability of ground prey, showing that prey switching matched to environmental dynamics plays a key role in covering the energy intake even in specialized predators.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the finding that gleaning provides 2.3-14 times higher prey profitability despite lower success rates (Figure 3F).

claim: Bats switch to aerial hunting when environmental changes reduce the profitability of ground prey.
source: We conclude that these bats use high risk-high gain gleaning of ground prey as a primary foraging tactic, but switch to aerial hunting when environmental changes reduce the profitability of ground prey, showing that prey switching matched to environmental dynamics plays a key role in covering the energy intake even in specialized predators.
evidence: This is supported by observations that on nights with more aerial captures, the time between gleaning attacks increased and strategy switching was more frequent.

claim: Prey switching matched to environmental dynamics plays a key role in covering the energy intake even in specialized predators.
source: We conclude that these bats use high risk-high gain gleaning of ground prey as a primary foraging tactic, but switch to aerial hunting when environmental changes reduce the profitability of ground prey, showing that prey switching matched to environmental dynamics plays a key role in covering the energy intake even in specialized predators.
evidence: This conclusion integrates findings on prey profitability, foraging success, and environmental influences on strategy choice.

claim: Predators are predicted to ignore low profitability prey when more profitable prey are present and abundant.
source: In these situations, predators are predicted to ignore low profitability prey when more profitable prey are present and abundant, and only switch prey type if there is a perceived prospect of increased profitability (i.e. more energy gained per time unit of hunting) (Stephens and Krebs, 1986).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from optimal foraging theory cited from Stephens and Krebs, 1986.

claim: Predators only switch prey type if there is a perceived prospect of increased profitability.
source: In these situations, predators are predicted to ignore low profitability prey when more profitable prey are present and abundant, and only switch prey type if there is a perceived prospect of increased profitability (i.e. more energy gained per time unit of hunting) (Stephens and Krebs, 1986).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from optimal foraging theory cited from Stephens and Krebs, 1986.

claim: Greater mouse-eared bats primarily capture ground-dwelling arthropods by passively listening for their movements (gleaning).
source: This species primarily captures ground-dwelling arthropods by passively listening for their movements (i.e. gleaning, Video 1; Video 2; Arlettaz, 1996), and is, therefore, specialized for gleaning: broad, short wings enable their take-off from the ground, and weak echolocation calls avoid alerting prey while also allowing the bat to hear rustling sounds of surface-dwelling prey.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Arlettaz, 1996 and videos showing gleaning behavior.

claim: Greater mouse-eared bats have broad, short wings that enable their take-off from the ground.
source: This species primarily captures ground-dwelling arthropods by passively listening for their movements (i.e. gleaning, Video 1; Video 2; Arlettaz, 1996), and is, therefore, specialized for gleaning: broad, short wings enable their take-off from the ground, and weak echolocation calls avoid alerting prey while also allowing the bat to hear rustling sounds of surface-dwelling prey.
evidence: This is a morphological characteristic associated with gleaning specialization.

claim: Greater mouse-eared bats have weak echolocation calls that avoid alerting prey while allowing the bat to hear rustling sounds of surface-dwelling prey.
source: This species primarily captures ground-dwelling arthropods by passively listening for their movements (i.e. gleaning, Video 1; Video 2; Arlettaz, 1996), and is, therefore, specialized for gleaning: broad, short wings enable their take-off from the ground, and weak echolocation calls avoid alerting prey while also allowing the bat to hear rustling sounds of surface-dwelling prey.
evidence: This is a sensory adaptation associated with gleaning specialization.

claim: Greater mouse-eared bats have maintained the ancestral ability to use echolocation to capture aerial prey on the wing (hawking).
source: Nonetheless, like many other gleaning bats, greater mouse-eared bats have maintained the ancestral ability to use echolocation to capture aerial prey on the wing (i.e. hawking, Video 3; Video 4; Video 5; Stidsholt et al., 2021), requiring that they switch to intense calls to detect small prey, and maintain the capability to maneuver fast in 3D space to track evasive prey.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stidsholt et al., 2021 and videos showing hawking behavior.

claim: All bats commuted from the colony or release site to one or several foraging grounds before returning back to the roost before dawn.
source: All bats commuted from the colony or release site to one or several foraging grounds before returning back to the roost before dawn (Figure 1ABC).
evidence: This is shown in the movement data from all 34 tagged bats displayed in Figure 1A-C.

claim: The bats attacked food more often on the ground (mean: 80 attacks per individual per night) than in the air (mean: 36 attacks).
source: The bats attacked food more often on the ground (mean: 80 attacks per individual per night, quartiles: 26–110) than in the air (mean: 36 attacks, quartiles: 7–70; GLMM, Poisson distribution, p=0.002, Supplementary file 1, Figure 1D), but the proportion of attacks that were successful (i.e. success ratio) based on audible mastication sounds following prey captures were more than double in the air (mean: 76%, quartiles: 71–88) than on ground (30%, quartiles: 25–40; Supplementary file 1, Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis (GLMM) of prey attack data from 34 bats, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The bats attacked prey more often on the ground (35 s between captures) compared to in the air (51 s between attacks).
source: The bats attacked prey more often on the ground (35 s between captures, quartiles: 17–70 s) compared to in the air (51 s between attacks, quartiles: 31–111, LMM, p<0.00001) (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis (LMM) of time between prey attacks, shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Almost half of all aerial prey was captured during commuting (47% of total aerial captures).
source: However, almost half of all aerial prey was captured during commuting (47% of total aerial captures; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is calculated from GPS-tagged bat data showing prey captures during different movement modes, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gleaning in open fields was twice as successful as in forest habitats (success ratio of 48% per foraging bout in open fields vs 12% in the forest).
source: Moreover, gleaning in open fields was twice as successful as in forest habitats (success ratio of 48% per foraging bout with more than two prey attacks in open fields vs 12% in the forest, Figure 2E, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis (LMM) of GPS-tagged bat data comparing success ratios across habitats, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: When capturing insects in the air, the attack rates and success ratios were consistently high and unaffected by habitat.
source: In contrast, when capturing insects in the air, the attack rates and success ratios were consistently high and unaffected by habitat (Figure 2DF, LMM, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis (LMM) showing no habitat effect on aerial hunting success, shown in Figure 2D and F.

claim: The bats target a wide range of prey species spanning 155 OUT (Operational Taxonomic Units).
source: The bats target a wide range of prey species spanning 155 OUT (Operational Taxonomic Units) (Figure 3AB), of which ~60% occupy aerial niches (36 families), and ~40% occupy ground niches (23 families; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on DNA metabarcoding analysis of feces from 54 bats, shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: ~60% of prey occupy aerial niches (36 families), and ~40% occupy ground niches (23 families).
source: The bats target a wide range of prey species spanning 155 OUT (Operational Taxonomic Units) (Figure 3AB), of which ~60% occupy aerial niches (36 families), and ~40% occupy ground niches (23 families; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on DNA metabarcoding analysis categorizing prey by habitat, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Ground prey was 2.5 times longer than aerial prey (20 mm vs 7 mm).
source: Ground prey was 2.5 x longer than aerial prey (20 mm (quartiles: 14–28 mm) vs 7 mm (quartiles 4–9 mm), Figure 3C) estimated from measured lengths of representatives of each species from online photo databases covering the same region in Bulgaria.
evidence: This is based on body length measurements from DNA metabarcoding data, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Estimated dry body masses of ground prey were ~20 times heavier than aerial prey (means: 67.5 mg vs 3.0 mg).
source: Under these assumptions, estimated dry body masses of ground prey were ~20 times heavier than aerial prey (means: 67.5 mg quartiles: 29.7–146.6 mg) vs 3.0 mg (quartiles: 0.7–5.7 mg, Figure 3E, green and blue circles).
evidence: This is calculated using length-weight regressions applied to DNA metabarcoding data, shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Bats chew longer on ground prey than aerial prey, indicated by ~3 times more mastication sounds detected after each gleaning capture (75) compared to aerial hawking (23).
source: Bats chew longer on ground prey than aerial prey, indicated by the ~3 x more mastication sounds detected after each gleaning capture (75, quartiles: 38.5–111.5, Figure 3D) compared to aerial hawking (23, quartiles: 15–55).
evidence: This is based on automatic detection of mastication sounds from tag recordings, shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The bats ingested an average of 60.2 kJ/night/bat based on the lower aerial prey body mass estimates.
source: Taking successful prey captures into account and the weighted average of the caloric values of the two most numerous prey types for aerial and ground (25.4 kJ/g dry mass of ground prey Bell, 1990; Zygmunt et al., 2006) and 21.3 kJ/g dry mass of aerial prey (Kurta and Kunz, 1987; Bell, 1990), the bats ingested an average of 60.2 kJ/night/bat (quartiles: 32.1–84.8) based on the lower aerial prey body mass estimates (Figure 3G, solid gray line), and 74.9 kJ/night/bat (quartiles: 55.2–95.7) based on the higher estimates (Figure 3G, shaded gray).
evidence: This is calculated from prey body mass estimates, caloric values from literature (Bell, 1990; Zygmunt et al., 2006; Kurta and Kunz, 1987), and capture success data, shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The bats ingested an average of 74.9 kJ/night/bat based on the higher aerial prey body mass estimates.
source: Taking successful prey captures into account and the weighted average of the caloric values of the two most numerous prey types for aerial and ground (25.4 kJ/g dry mass of ground prey Bell, 1990; Zygmunt et al., 2006) and 21.3 kJ/g dry mass of aerial prey (Kurta and Kunz, 1987; Bell, 1990), the bats ingested an average of 60.2 kJ/night/bat (quartiles: 32.1–84.8) based on the lower aerial prey body mass estimates (Figure 3G, solid gray line), and 74.9 kJ/night/bat (quartiles: 55.2–95.7) based on the higher estimates (Figure 3G, shaded gray).
evidence: This is calculated from prey body mass estimates, caloric values from literature (Bell, 1990; Zygmunt et al., 2006; Kurta and Kunz, 1987), and capture success data, shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Using energy assimilation rates of 50–82% in bats, the bats obtained on average between 30–61 kJ/night per bat.
source: Using energy assimilation rates of 50–82% in bats (Kurta et al., 1989; Straus and Avilés, 2018), the bats obtained on average between 30–61 kJ/night per bat (Figure 3G) during the hunting seasons of July to August.
evidence: This is calculated by applying assimilation rates from literature (Kurta et al., 1989; Straus and Avilés, 2018) to the estimated energy intake, shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The gleaning foraging strategy yielded a profitability of 7.4 J/s.
source: The gleaning foraging strategy yielded a profitability of 7.4 J/s (quartiles: 5.6–8.1 J/s, Figure 3F green), while hawking resulted in a lower estimate of 0.5 J/s (quartiles: 0.4–0.54, Figure 3F, blue circles) and a higher estimate of 3.3 J/s (quartiles: 2.8–3.8, Figure 3F, blue triangles).
evidence: This is calculated by combining success ratios, search and handling times, and prey body mass estimates, shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Hawking resulted in a lower profitability estimate of 0.5 J/s and a higher estimate of 3.3 J/s.
source: The gleaning foraging strategy yielded a profitability of 7.4 J/s (quartiles: 5.6–8.1 J/s, Figure 3F green), while hawking resulted in a lower estimate of 0.5 J/s (quartiles: 0.4–0.54, Figure 3F, blue circles) and a higher estimate of 3.3 J/s (quartiles: 2.8–3.8, Figure 3F, blue triangles).
evidence: This is calculated by combining success ratios, search and handling times, and prey body mass estimates, shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Prey profitability when gleaning is 2.3–14 times higher than when aerial hawking.
source: Prey profitability when gleaning is thus 2.3–14 times higher than when aerial hawking.
evidence: This is calculated from the profitability estimates for gleaning (7.4 J/s) and hawking (0.5-3.3 J/s) shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The high success ratios for greater mouse-eared bats when hawking are on par with observations in the wild for hawking specialist bats.
source: Surprisingly, the high success ratios for greater mouse-eared bats when hawking are on par with observations in the wild for hawking specialist bats (Rydell et al., 2002).
evidence: This comparison is made to literature on hawking specialist bats (Rydell et al., 2002).

claim: During one night of foraging, the bats on average caught a mean of 25 insects in the air and 29 insects on the ground.
source: During one night of foraging, the bats on average caught a mean of 25 insects in the air and 29 insects on the ground (Figure 1) demonstrating a reliance on both food sources.
evidence: This is based on prey capture data from 34 tagged bats, shown in Figure 1.

claim: These numbers are on par with total prey captures of the similar-sized Rhinopoma microphyllum, estimated from buzz counts.
source: These numbers are on par with total prey captures of the similar-sized Rhinopoma microphyllum, estimated from buzz counts (Cvikel et al., 2015), but well below the very high feeding rates inferred in a smaller (7–11 g) species (M. daubentonii) (Encarnação and Dietz, 2006).
evidence: This comparison is made to literature on other bat species (Cvikel et al., 2015; Encarnação and Dietz, 2006).

claim: Wild greater mouse-eared bats in this study assimilated an average of 61.4 kJ/night per bat (assuming 82% assimilation).
source: Given our measured total prey captures and prey sizes, wild greater mouse-eared bats in our study assimilated an average of 61.4 kJ/night per bat (assuming 82% assimilation) (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is calculated from prey capture and size data with an assumed assimilation rate, shown in Figure 3G.

claim: This is higher than the estimated field metabolic rate (FMR) of the similar-sized female lesser long-nosed bats (Leptonycteris yerbabuenae) of 40 kJ/day.
source: This is higher than the estimated field metabolic rate (FMR) of the similar-sized female lesser long-nosed bats (Leptonycteris yerbabuenae) of 40 kJ/day (Goldshtein et al., 2020), but close to the allometric scaling estimate of the FMR of a 30 g bat based on heart rate measurements from wild-tagged 18 g Uroderma bilobatum (FMRM.myo = FMRU.bil * (30 g/18 g)0.7 = 65.5 kJ/day) (O'Mara et al., 2017).
evidence: This comparison is made to FMR estimates from literature (Goldshtein et al., 2020; O'Mara et al., 2017).

claim: The estimated food intake of the tagged bats matches their predicted FMR.
source: Thus, despite making less than 100 prey captures per night, the estimated food intake of the tagged bats matches their predicted FMR.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the calculated energy intake (61.4 kJ/night) to the predicted FMR (65.5 kJ/day) from O'Mara et al., 2017.

claim: Tagged bats attacked from 48 to 280 prey during a night of foraging.
source: Moreover, despite selecting only heavy, post-lactating females within the same colony, we measured a wide individual variation in hunting tactics. Tagged bats attacked from 48 to 280 prey during a night of foraging (Figures 1 and 2), demonstrating that continuous recordings from the same individuals are important to quantify the hunting efforts and energy budgets of wild predators, and that extrapolations of food intake from brief observations may result in significant errors in that light.
evidence: This is based on prey attack data from 34 tagged bats, shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Gleaning insects most likely exposes bats to a higher predation risks from ground predators, and a higher risk of injury.
source: Moreover, gleaning insects most likely exposes bats to a higher predation risks from ground predators, and a higher risk of injury ( Brandmayr, 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the nature of ground foraging and cited from Brandmayr, 2009.

claim: Beetles gleaned off the ground are 3–20 times heavier than aerial prey and have higher protein and fat content.
source: Beetles gleaned off the ground are 3–20 times heavier than aerial prey and have higher protein and fat content (Razeng and Watson, 2015).
evidence: This is based on prey body mass estimates from this study and nutritional content cited from Razeng and Watson, 2015.

claim: Aerial hunting remains as a valuable supportive foraging strategy for 19 out of 34 individuals on the nights sampled, contributing 15% of the total energy intake.
source: Nevertheless, we find that aerial hunting remains as a valuable supportive foraging strategy for 19 out of 34 individuals on the nights sampled (Figure 1DE), contributing 15% of the total energy intake.
evidence: This is calculated from prey capture and energy intake data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Bats primarily gleaned prey during dedicated foraging bouts, whereas hawking was used equally during commute and in foraging bouts.
source: The bats primarily gleaned prey during dedicated foraging bouts, whereas hawking was used equally during commute and in foraging bouts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of GPS-tagged bat data showing prey captures during different movement modes, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Aerial hawking is a flexible strategy that is efficient enough to use during commuting.
source: This indicates that aerial hawking is a flexible strategy that is efficient enough to use during commuting.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that hawking was used equally during commute and foraging bouts.

claim: When actively gleaning for prey, the tagged bats were more successful and attacked more prey per bout in open fields than in forest habitats (26 vs 15 attacks/bout).
source: When actively gleaning for prey, the tagged bats were more successful and attacked more prey per bout in open fields than in forest habitats (26 vs 15 attacks/bout), but performed more foraging bouts in the forest (field: eight foraging bouts vs forest: 15 bouts; three bouts were a mixture between field and forest).
evidence: This is based on analysis of GPS-tagged bat data comparing foraging behavior across habitats.

claim: Bats performed more foraging bouts in the forest (field: eight foraging bouts vs forest: 15 bouts).
source: When actively gleaning for prey, the tagged bats were more successful and attacked more prey per bout in open fields than in forest habitats (26 vs 15 attacks/bout), but performed more foraging bouts in the forest (field: eight foraging bouts vs forest: 15 bouts; three bouts were a mixture between field and forest).
evidence: This is based on analysis of GPS-tagged bat data comparing foraging behavior across habitats.

claim: Bats were equally successful when using echolocation to capture insects above open fields and below the canopy in forests.
source: In contrast to gleaning, bats were equally successful when using echolocation to capture insects above open fields and below the canopy in forests showing that these bats are well able to hunt in semi-cluttered spaces (Stidsholt et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on analysis of GPS-tagged bat data showing no habitat effect on aerial hunting success, with citation to Stidsholt et al., 2021.

claim: The dominant foraging strategies of individuals tagged on the same night were more similar than those for bats tagged on different nights.
source: Although greater mouse-eared bats hunt independently, the dominant foraging strategies of individuals tagged on the same night were more similar than those for bats tagged on different nights.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis (LMM) showing that the night of tagging explained the ratio between ground and aerial captures (Supplementary file 1g).

claim: Temporally-varying environmental parameters such as rain, wind, or mass emergence of aerial insects, experienced by all bats in the area on a given night, influence the most beneficial foraging strategy.
source: This indicates that temporally-varying environmental parameters such as rain, wind, or mass emergence of aerial insects, experienced by all bats in the area on a given night, influence the most beneficial foraging strategy.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that bats tagged on the same night chose similar foraging strategies.

claim: After rain, the rustling sounds of walking arthropods on leaves are more difficult for bats to detect potentially halving the detection range.
source: For example, after rain, the rustling sounds of walking arthropods on leaves are more difficult for bats to detect potentially halving the detection range (Goerlitz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Goerlitz et al., 2008.

claim: The time between gleaning prey attacks increased by an average of 35 s on the two nights with the most aerial captures.
source: The time between gleaning prey attacks increased by an average of 35 s on the two nights with the most aerial captures (July 22, 2018 and 2019, GLMM; testing whether the time between gleaning attacks was explained by nights with a majority of aerial captures, p<0.01) and the bats switched more often between gleaning and aerial strategies on an attack-to-attack basis (GLMM; testing if the number of switches per night was explained by the nights with a majority of aerial captures, p<0.01).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis (GLMM) of prey attack timing data.

claim: The bats switched more often between gleaning and aerial strategies on an attack-to-attack basis on nights with a majority of aerial captures.
source: The time between gleaning prey attacks increased by an average of 35 s on the two nights with the most aerial captures (July 22, 2018 and 2019, GLMM; testing whether the time between gleaning attacks was explained by nights with a majority of aerial captures, p<0.01) and the bats switched more often between gleaning and aerial strategies on an attack-to-attack basis (GLMM; testing if the number of switches per night was explained by the nights with a majority of aerial captures, p<0.01).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis (GLMM) of strategy switching data.

claim: The consistently high success ratios and prey capture rates of hawking independent of habitat make this a reliable backup strategy.
source: Although much smaller prey are taken on the wing, the consistently high success ratios and prey capture rates of hawking independent of habitat make this a reliable backup strategy.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing high and consistent hawking success across habitats (Figure 2D, F).

claim: Foraging flexibility both adds to the energy intake of wild bats and also improves their resilience to changing conditions.
source: Such foraging flexibility both adds to the energy intake of wild bats and also improves their resilience to changing conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings on prey switching and energy intake.

claim: This strategy might have allowed a wide range of bat species to tap into the unpredictable, ephemeral food resources in open spaces.
source: Thus, this strategy might have allowed a wide range of bat species to tap into the unpredictable, ephemeral food resources in open spaces.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the evolutionary implications of foraging flexibility.

claim: This would have put an evolutionary pressure on maintaining aerial hawking capabilities to secure an additional food resource in fluctuating environments.
source: This would have put an evolutionary pressure on maintaining aerial hawking capabilities to secure an additional food resource in fluctuating environments, and may also explain why hawking remains as a foraging strategy in many bat species traditionally seen as gleaning and trawling specialists.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about evolutionary pressures based on the study findings.

claim: Prey availability and size, weighted by relative hunting success, are important drivers of foraging decisions in wild predators.
source: This shows that prey availability and size, weighted by relative hunting success, are important drivers of foraging decisions in wild predators.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings on prey profitability and foraging strategy choice.

claim: Bats use gleaning as a primary foraging tactic in a high risk-high gain approach.
source: We find that the bats use gleaning as a primary foraging tactic in a high risk-high gain approach, and switch to aerial hunting when environmental changes reduce the profitability of ground prey.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings on prey profitability, success ratios, and strategy switching.

claim: 34 female, post-lactating greater mouse-eared bats were tagged with sound-and-movement tags from late July to mid-August in the seasons 2017, 2018, and 2019.
source: We tagged and recaptured 34 female, post-lactating greater mouse-eared bats with sound-and-movement tags from late July to mid-August in the seasons 2017, 2018, and 2019.
evidence: This describes the study methodology.

claim: The bats were caught with a harp trap at Orlova Chuka cave, close to Ruse, NE-Bulgaria.
source: The bats were caught with a harp trap at Orlova Chuka cave, close to Ruse, NE-Bulgaria, in the early mornings as they returned to the roost.
evidence: This describes the study methodology.

claim: Two different tags were used for this study, both recording continuous data during one night of foraging.
source: We used two different tags for this study. Both tags recorded continuous data during one night of foraging.
evidence: This describes the study methodology.

claim: Both tags weighed 11–15% of the body weight of the tagged bats.
source: Both tags weighed 11–15% of the body weight of the tagged bats.
evidence: This describes the study methodology.

claim: Tagged and un-tagged trained bats quickly learned to intercept aerial and ground prey in the lab with similar success ratios as in the wild.
source: The bats caught aerial prey with high success ratios (95% for mealworms and 69% for moths (N=2 bats)) with tags and without tags (75% for mealworms (N=4 bats)). The bats gleaned beetles with a success ratio of 39% from the square of the forest floor. The success ratio increased to 85% when they were catching beetles from a bowl with no escape options for the prey (N=3 bats). This indicates that the low gleaning success ratios in the wild are most likely not caused by tagging effects, but more likely because beetles can escape in cracks or below leaves.
evidence: This is based on laboratory experiments to assess tagging effects.

claim: The weight loss of these bats of 7% during the instrumentation time was equal to the weight loss of control bats carrying only VHF radio transmitters (0.5 g).
source: (iv) The weight loss of these bats of 7% during the instrumentation time was equal to the weight loss of control bats carrying only VHF radio transmitters (0.5 g) indicating that handling and carrying of tags might disturb the bats, but the additional extra load did not seem to add further energetic consequences to the bats in addition to the VHF (Egert-Berg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on comparison to control bats with lighter transmitters, cited from Egert-Berg et al., 2018.

claim: DNA metabarcoding was performed on the feces of 54 untagged greater mouse-eared bats from the same colony caught in the morning upon returning from the foraging grounds.
source: To estimate prey types and sizes, we first performed DNA metabarcoding analysis on the feces of 54 untagged greater mouse-eared bats from the same colony caught in the morning upon returning from the foraging grounds.
evidence: This describes the study methodology for prey identification.

claim: Greater mouse-eared bats chew all prey while flying irrespective of how they are caught.
source: Greater mouse-eared bats chew all prey while flying irrespective of how they are caught and take longer to masticate larger prey (verified in laboratory feeding experiments, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is verified in laboratory feeding experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Greater mouse-eared bats take longer to masticate larger prey.
source: Greater mouse-eared bats chew all prey while flying irrespective of how they are caught and take longer to masticate larger prey (verified in laboratory feeding experiments, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is verified in laboratory feeding experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bats are widespread and abundant predators that serve important roles in ecosystems across the globe.
source: Bats are widespread and abundant predators that serve important roles in ecosystems across the globe (Kunz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Kunz et al., 2011.

claim: The evolutionary success of bats is due to the unique combination of echolocation and powered flight.
source: Their evolutionary success is due to the unique combination of echolocation and powered flight (Teeling et al., 2005) allowing them to avoid visual predators by feeding at night, thereby gaining unfettered access to food sources that include insects, small vertebrates, fruit, nectar, pollen, and blood (Simmons, 2005).
evidence: This is cited from Teeling et al., 2005 and Simmons, 2005.

claim: Echolocating bats are categorized into three main foraging strategies: hawking, trawling, and gleaning.
source: Within the mosaic of foraging niches they exploit, echolocating bats are categorized into three main foraging strategies: the ancestral mode of capturing prey on the wing (hawking), and the derived modes of trawling prey from water surfaces or gleaning prey, nectar, or fruit from ground and trees (Schnitzler and Kalko, 2001).
evidence: This is cited from Schnitzler and Kalko, 2001.

claim: Each guild of bats has evolved specific adaptations in echolocation signals, auditory systems, morphology, and flight mechanics to aid specialized hunting strategies.

claim: Foraging style is not monotypic within species: gleaning bats occasionally capture aerial prey.
source: Despite such specialism, recent research has shown that foraging style is not monotypic within species: gleaning bats occasionally capture aerial prey (Bell, 1982; Fenton, 1990; Ratcliffe and Dawson, 2003; Ratcliffe et al., 2006; Hackett et al., 2014), while insect-gleaning bats may seasonally target nectar or fruit (Aliperti et al., 2017) or vice versa (Herrera M. et al., 2001).
